paras: Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.

In a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category.

The priority, of course, is to get the actual film, Bond 26, up and running. Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight, who has been hired to write the script, says he has delivered his first draft – but if previous iterations of the series are anything to go by, there are likely to be copious notes, rewrites, and other writers hauled into the process. It is the Bond movie’s special curse that it needs to be immediately comprehensible to global audiences while putatively delivering a labyrinthine narrative of bluff and counterbluff, contain several massive action set pieces and a handful of drawn-out romantic and/or sexual encounters.

It has also got used to providing ample product placement and branding opportunities, although it is yet to be seen whether Amazon MGM will continue with this method of covering the film’s budget. In recent years, Bond has faced a tonal challenge too: retaining its customary small-c conservatism while attempting to grapple with more modern ideas about PTSD and sexism.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/commentis.desc: I am at Cop31 – concerned about the crisis around the world, but mindful that voters want jobs, warmer homes and cheaper prices, says energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh
paras: In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.

That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. And yet, the Conservatives and Reform UK want to bury their heads in the sand and break the consensus on delivering net zero. But we know sustained climate action can work.

Yes, the world will overshoot 1.5C of global heating in the coming years. But without the Paris agreement, the world would have been on track for a 4C increase. International commitments, finance and adaptation are working, and multilateralism has never been more vital to our future. Every fraction of a degree we prevent means lives protected and communities given a better chance at surviving. Setbacks bring frustration, but resistance is the sign of progress.

pg:https://www.theguardian.com/society/2.desc: Former minister’s 278-page report calls for changes to employment regulations, education, healthcare and benefits

While this was in part covered by the first report, Milburn is at pains to begin the new volume with his belief that the issue of Neets is not a failure of the younger generation but a case of them being let down by a series of structural factors. “The young people I have met over the last year are not asking for an easier life. They are asking for a fair chance to build one,” he writes.

The answer must be radical, he says. “This cannot be fixed by tweaking the edges of the existing system. The response now has to be full throttle: not another initiative or another round of incremental reform, but transformational change.”

pg:https://www.nj.gov/health/news/2026/a.desc: Statement on Loss of Measles Elimination Status in the United States
paras: TRENTON, NJ – Today, the Pan-American Health Organization has officially revoked our nation’s measles elimination status. The loss of this status in the U.S. is a sobering reminder that decades of public health progress can be undone in a short fraction of that time and should not be taken for granted.

Losing elimination status represents a significant setback – and a preventable one. Public health and medical experts have repeatedly raised concerns about declining vaccination rates. When less than 95% of a community is vaccinated against measles, the virus can spread quickly. According to the most recent data, only 92% of children in New Jersey have received the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine by 24 months of age, on par with 91.4% nationally. According to the latest data, vaccination coverage among kindergartners in the U.S. is 92.4% for MMR vaccine, below herd immunity.

Public health is about prevention and keeping communities healthier. The New Jersey Department of Health (NJDOH) remains steadfast in its commitment to increasing access to lifesaving immunizations, which continue to be our most effective tools against preventable illnesses and protecting health.

It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.

paras: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 was meant to study the gas giants of our solar system, Jupiter and Saturn. But by 1998, it continued on past them, becoming the farthest human-made object ever. It reached interstellar space — the region just outside the sun’s magnetic influence known as the heliopause — back in 2012, at a distance of 18 billion kilometres. Now, it’s more than 26 billion kilometres away.

Arguably, being a “light day” away is an arbitrary threshold, as there’s no new physical boundary or change to Voyager 1 itself. But experts say it’s remarkable because it’s still plugging along on its mission while communicating with Earth.

Voyager 1’s power is generated by the heat from the natural decay of plutonium. As that power has dwindled over nearly half a century, most of its science instruments have been shut down, the latest being the LCEP, which measured low-energy charged particles. There are two instruments that still work, one for measuring plasma waves and the other for magnetic fields.

NASA expects it to have reached that milestone at 5:16:07 AM Eastern time today, November 18. One light-day is the distance a particle of light can travel in a day. Since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours to send a command to the probe and 24 hours to get a message back. That's why NASA won't be able to confirm exactly what time it reached one light-day away until tomorrow, when the probe's message arrives.

Voyager 1 headed to space in 1977 as part of NASA's program to study not just our Solar System, but also interstellar space. It was launched 16 days after Voyager 2, but it has since traveled farther than its twin and any other probe we've sent out. Voyager 1 reached interstellar space — that's the region between star systems — back in 2012, before Voyager 2 did. It suffered technical glitches, and NASA had to shut down some of its features to keep it going despite the diminishing plutonium in its generator. But it's still around and hasn't stopped its journey.

After traveling for 49 years, two months and 11 days, it's now believed to be about 16 billion miles from our planet—and it's not done yet. Voyager 1 is headed toward a star called Gliese 445, about 17 light-years from Earth in the Ursa Minor constellation. In terms of space distances, that's not so far away. However, none of us would be here by the time it reaches that goal: It's expected to pass within 1.7 light-years of Gliese 445 in 40,000 years.

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 18 (Xinhua) -- NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft reached a distance of one light-day from Earth on Wednesday, becoming the first human-made object to travel so far into space, NASA said on its official Voyager mission website.

According to NASA's calculations, the milestone occurred at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern Time on Wednesday. One light-day is the distance a particle of light can travel in 24 hours, equivalent to about 26 billion kilometers.

Launched in 1977 to fly by Jupiter and Saturn, Voyager 1 has been traveling through space for nearly 50 years. Its twin spacecraft, Voyager 2, followed a different trajectory through the solar system to explore Uranus and Neptune. Voyager 2 is expected to reach the one-light-day distance from Earth in November 2035, NASA said.
